articles.title: Happy Thanksgiving: Patents for the Turkey, Cranberries and Pie
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Happy Thanksgiving from Patently-O. Four patent drawings for the holiday, with a bit of color added. The first is Itura Leigh’s “Toy Representing a Turkey Gobbler,” U.S. Patent No. 1,678,226 (1928). Leigh, of Grantville, Georgia, built her gobbler from “an ordinary pine burr” — a pine cone — with the scales of a second cone glued in to make the strutting tail. The legs are four strands of wire wrapped in red tissue paper, the head and neck are papier-mâché with black beads for eyes, and a tassel of black wool hangs from the base of the neck.
The colors here are hers: “I prefer to color the neck red and the head white and purple.” Her single claim requires “an entire pine cone,” and the specification promises that the finished toy “at a short distance appears a close imitation to the natural bird.”
Leigh was better known in Grantville as “Miss Love.” Born Itura Moreland, she “finished” at Wesleyan College in 1884, married the next year, but was “left a widow early in life” with four sons. She later remarried S.E. Leigh.
Beginning about 1924 she ran a cottage business called Loveleigh Novelties out of Bonnie Castle, the Colley family’s brick mansion in Grantville (shown above). The main product was a line of handmade character dolls with walnut heads and wire bodies wrapped in cloth or crepe paper — the same wire-and-paper construction as the turkey’s legs. A 1998 University of Delaware alumni magazine profile of the house (then a bed and breakfast) describes “patented dolls that enjoyed an international market.” The turkey is the only patent I have found in her name. Most of the surviving examples of her dolls are Black character figures in stereotyped roles. In 1929, a year after the patent issued, the Wesleyan alumnae magazine ran a sketch of Leigh as its first lifetime donor – she had pledged “ten dollars or more each January for the rest of my life.”
Cranberries (1865). Charles Thacher of Yarmouth, Massachusetts received U.S. Patent No. 48,136 in June 1865 for an “Improved Cranberry-Gatherer,” less than two years after Lincoln’s 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation. This is a Cape Cod cranberry scoop: a box-shaped receiver with a toothed bottom that is pushed into the vines. A hinged “holding-comb” then swings down onto the teeth, and the whole apparatus is drawn back “so as to strip the berries from the vines.” Tipping the box causes the berries to roll across a grate “so as to sift from them any extraneous matters.”
Thacher had a partner. Three months earlier, George Shove received U.S. Patent No. 46,760, also titled “Improved Cranberry-Gatherer,” and assigned it “to himself and Thacher, of same place.” Thacher’s patent does the same – assigned to himself and Shove.
The turkey costume (2024). U.S. Design Patent No. D1,021,329 claims “the ornamental design for a turkey costume, as shown and described” – a hooded one-piece with a scalloped fan under each arm, a scalloped bib at the collar, and a buckled Pilgrim hat. The patent issued April 2024 to Henan Queqiaoxian Electronic Technology Co. of Zhengzhou, China, less than four months after its December 2023 filing date. The same inventor, Chengen Zhang, patented a “Mothman costume” (D1,030,235) that I’ll save for next year’s Halloween edition. The prior art cited by the examiner includes two turkey onesies sold on Amazon. The patented costume itself is for sale on Amazon, and I have roughly matched its colors here.
Dessert (2025). U.S. Design Patent No. D1,077,414 claims “the ornamental design for a pie, as shown and described.” You can see in the figure below that it is a pie divided up into three wedges. The outline of the pie is drawn in broken lines and so is not part of the claimed design. I have colored the wedges as pecan, pumpkin and cherry, but the patent does not actually name a filling. For a three-filling pie you can actually order, Anna Bananas Bakery in Manahawkin, New Jersey is selling a “Tri Pie” this Thanksgiving: apple, blueberry and cherry, with a crumb topping.
Enjoy the holiday.

articles.title: Issue Fee to Grant: Record Weekly Patent Issues Are a USPTO Catch-Up
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

The USPTO issued 9,828 utility patents on November 3, 2026 -- the largest weekly issue in records back to 1976. The three issues since then (November 10, 17 and 24) rank second through fourth. Before November, the record was 7,837 on October 3, 2023.

These high numbers are really a catch-up on the part of the patent office. In October I wrote that the wait from issue-fee payment to grant had doubled due to a surge in fee filing earlier in the year. It is now coming back down: 49 days for the November 24 issue and I expect further decreases moving forward.

articles.title: How to Change the Name Shown on Patently-O Comments
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

Patently-O members can now choose the name shown on their comments. The site calls it your public name. This allows folks to post comments without using their actual name.

To change it, sign in and go to your account page. A box headed "Public name" sits under your profile on the Home tab. Type the name you want in the "New public name" field and click "Save name." There is also a "Change your public name" link on the comment form itself.

To continue reading, become a Patently-O member. Already a member? Simply log in to access the full post.

articles.title: Following the Footnotes: How Enablement Became a Question of Law
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit regularly says that enablement is a question of law based upon underlying facts -- stated again in Satius v. Samsung (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), one of about 130 majority opinions restating the rule. The label lets the appellate court decide enablement de novo and largely disregard the jury's verdict. A famous recent example comes from Amgen v. Sanofi, where the jury found the antibody claims enabled, but the district court and then the Federal Circuit set the verdict aside. But, the nineteenth-century Supreme Court generally treated sufficiency of a patent's description as a question of fact for the jury, not a question of law. Wood v. Underhill (1846).
In about 115 of those 130 opinions, the citation chain leads back to one footnote: Raytheon v. Roper, 724 F.2d 951, 960 n.6 (Fed. Cir. 1983). The footnote is one sentence with no reasoning:
Enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112, paragraph 1, is a question of law.
That one sentence is followed by a string-cite of C.C.P.A. opinion-affidavit cases. The string ends with In re Chilowsky (C.C.P.A. 1962), which makes the matter-of-law claim but cites no source of precedent. (I looked at the other cases in the string-cite as well. None of them explains why enablement is a question of law.) The first, and perhaps only, real explanation I found in a Federal Circuit opinion came 37 years after Raytheon, in Judge Lourie's nonprecedential 2021 opinion denying panel rehearing in Amgen. In my view, the court owes an explanation.

articles.title: Rule 17 Real Party in Interest: No Swapping the Original Plaintiff Back After a Tactical Substitution
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal with prejudice of a patent suit against Netflix -- holding that a plaintiff who swapped-in a newly formed LLC to get around a problem with its own corporate status could not swap itself back once the new LLC turned out to lack the right to sue. Rule 17(a)(3) protects the honest mistake about who should be the plaintiff, but the district court found that this one was "done for tactical advantage."
Touchmusic sued Netflix in March 2024, asserting US6182128, which had expired almost six years earlier. But, at the time of filing Touchmusic's corporate rights were suspended under California law, and a suspended company is barred from filing suit. "This did not deter Touchmusic." Rather than dismissing the case, Touchmusic assigned the patent to newly formed Ziklag IP, a Tennessee LLC, and filed an amended complaint to replace Touchmusic with Ziklag as plaintiff. California restored Touchmusic's good standing on April 19, 2024 - one day after the assignment.
The assignment appears complete on its face:
Touchmusic "hereby irrevocably conveys, transfers, and assigns all of Touchmusic's right, title, and interest in and to the Patent to Ziklag IP LLC."
But assignment of patent rights does not typically confer rights to sue for infringement that occurred before the assignment - that right is still held by the prior owner unless expressly transferred.
